name: South Andaman / Aka-Bea
confidence_why: Man and Ellis's alphabet rule (Man 1885, repeated in Man 1923) and Temple 1903 put Aka-Bea stress on a long vowel or diphthong and otherwise on the first syllable of the root, and Zamponi and Comrie 2021 likewise describe Great Andamanese stress as non-contrastive and ordinarily root-initial, but Blevins 2009 reads Man's stress marks as unpredictable, and Zamponi and Comrie's 2020 Akabea grammar, which treats stress directly, has not been consulted.

new_statements.quote: RULE. In the above alphabet the syllable under stress in any word is shown by placing a turned period (·) after a long vowel, or the consonant following a short vowel, in every word of more than one syllable. [examples on the same page: al·aba 'kind of tree', elà·kà 'region', jär·awa 'name of a tribe', yâ·ba 'not', ig-bû dig-re 'see-did', chôpau·a 'narrow', tô·go 'wrist, shoulder', bû·kura 'name of a tree', êrkê·dang-ke 'in trees-search-does', râ·ta 'wooden arrow', ṛâ·ta 'sea-water', wô·lo 'adze', yabâ· 'a little', mû·gu 'face', rô·pan 'toad'] — vertxt-3 excerpt, sentence 33 note: "ba at the end is a contraction for yába, and never becomes bâ (meaning 'small'), but is kept short and unaccented"

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 2 pages), rendered leaf 1 at 200 dpi and read it. Printed p. 3 'ALPHABET FOR WRITING THE SOUTH ANDAMAN LANGUAGE', paragraph headed 'RULE.' reads exactly: 'In the above alphabet the syllable under stress in any word is shown by placing a turned period (·) after a long vowel, or the consonant following a short vowel, in every word of more than one syllable.' The IA scanned carries the same sentence. The bracketed example list has small transcription slips: the page prints 'ig-bâ dig-re' (not 'ig-bû'), and neither it nor 'nàu-ke' shows a visible turned period; 'yabā·' and 'yā·ba' carry a macron on the page, not a circumflex; 'bal·awa name of a tribe' is on the page but not in the compiler list…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for akab1249 has an empty rule and no existing statements; Man 1923 supplies the primary-source practice (per-word stress marking, no rule, variable position). It also bears on the family-wide statement already held by the project from Zamponi & Comrie 2021 (A Grammar of Akajeru, p. 22: stress non-phonemic, 'falls on the initial syllable of the root, at least ordinarily'): most of Man's marks are root-initial once prefixes (ig-, êr-, e-) are discounted, but yâ·ba 'not' vs yabâ· 'a little' shows lexically fixed non-initial stress, which is what Blevins 2009 (p. 5, held by the project) reads as 'does not appear to be predictable, although final syllable stress is rare'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Man gives no placement rule: stress is a property of each polysyllabic word and is written word by word with a turned period (after a long vowel, or after the consonant closing a short-vowel syllable). His examples put it mostly on the first syllable of the root (al·aba, tô·go, bû·kura, râ·ta, wô·lo, mû·gu; after a prefix in ig-bû dig-re, êrkê·dang-ke, elà·kà), but also non-initially (chôpau·a 'narrow') and finally (yabâ· 'a little', contrasting with yâ·ba 'not'). Unstressed enclitic -ba (< yába) is 'kept short and unaccented'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; in compounds/phrases each root carries its own mark (ig-bû dig-re, êrkê·dang-ke).
new_statements.exceptions: No rule, so no exceptions stated; the marked data include final stress (yabâ· 'a little', àweh·) and second-syllable stress (chôpau·a) beside the predominant root-initial pattern. The item is a 2-leaf excerpt (title page + p. 3); the full dictionary is not on archive.org (advancedsearch found only the Rosetta excerpts), and the other excerpts (introduction/morphology-syntax, verb texts, numbers, vocabulary) contain no further stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Man 1923 describes Aka-Bea (South Andaman, 'âkà-bêa-da'), the variety of the catalog entry; the orthography page and Ellis's texts are Aka-Bea. Zamponi & Comrie 2021's statement (held by the project) is about the Great Andamanese family as a whole, made in a grammar of Akajeru (akaj1239), and is applied to Akabea by the authors' own wording.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is predictable on the first syllable of the root.26 This is indicated by Temple: The accent, as a rule, falls on the first syllable of the base; prefixes and affixes are never accentuated (Temple 1877: 9) [fn. 26:] The absence of stress marking suggests that compound words consisting of a single phonological word are stressed on the first syllable of the first root (e.g. pɔ́ʧo (<pāūcho>; PM: 206) 'k.o. bamboo and cane knife'). [p. 59:] The absence of stress marking in the Akabea words recorded in PN is a further indication that word stress is fixed in the position indicated above ... A line is placed under a syllable to show the stress on it. When a word is not so marked the stress should be placed on the first syllable (PN: 29).

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has Aka-Bea as 'weight-hedged' with no rule, and the existing statement (Man 1923 p. 3 marking rule) was read as lexical/unpredictable because Man marks the stressed syllable in every polysyllable. Zamponi & Comrie state the opposite type: stress is predictable, root-initial (first syllable of the root, affixes never stressed), citing Temple 1877 and Portman's default-first-syllable convention. Man's turned-period convention is a transcription device and does not itself assert unpredictability; Z&C's analysis of the same corpus (Portman, Man, Temple) concludes fixed root-initial stress. No weight sensitivity is mentioned.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fixed and predictable: it falls on the first syllable of the root (base). Prefixes (e.g. the somatic prefixes, the gender prefix aka-) and suffixes are never stressed, so in prefixed words stress is not word-initial. Compounds forming a single phonological word take stress on the first syllable of the first root. The authors also note (fn. 10, p. 51) that 'the accented syllable.. is always the first syllable of the root in Akabea', and (p. 56) that Portman's long-vowel marks on root-initial syllables probably record stress rather than length.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Akabea; Portman's underline stress-marking convention was 'de facto applied exclusively to a few Okol and Okojuwoi items' (p. 59), i.e. the marked exceptions belong to other Great Andamanese varieties, not Akabea.
new_statements.identity_note: The chapter describes Akabea (Aka-Bea, South Andaman) as reconstructed from 19th/early-20th c. records (Portman, Man, Temple); the few stress-marked exceptions Portman recorded belong to Okol and Okojuwoi, other Great Andamanese varieties, not Akabea.

readall_conflicts: Two expert readings of Man's marks disagree. Zamponi & Comrie 2021 (Akajeru grammar, sec. 2.2, p. 22; already held by the project in our files) state for the whole Great Andamanese family incl. Akabea that stress is not phonemically relevant and non-phonemic stress falls on the initial syllable of the root 'at least ordinarily'; their 2020 Akabea grammar ch. 2 (pp. 43-68, paywalled, not opened) covers stress explicitly. Blevins 2009 (p. 5, held by the project) reads Man's marks as unpredictable with rare final stress. his p. 3 examples are mostly root-initial (including after prefixes: ig-bû dig-re, êrkê·dang-ke, elà·kà) with a few non-initial/final cases (chôpau·a, yabâ· 'a little' vs yâ·ba 'not', àweh·). So the type question (non-contrastive root-initial vs lexically fixed) is unresolved between Z&C and Blevins; the placement facts are compatible with Z&C's 'root-initial, ordinarily' plus a handful of lexical exceptions. The only modern analytic source, Zamponi & Comrie 2020 (ch. 2, section 2.4, pp. 58-59), states that Akabea word stress is predictable on the first syllable of the root, with prefixes and suffixes never stressed (after Temple 1877: 9) and compounds stressed on the first root. This conflicts with the catalog's 'weight-hedged' kind and with the earlier reading of Man 1923's orthographic rule (p. 3) as 'lexical (unpredictable)': Man's rule only says that the stressed syllable is marked with a turned period in every polysyllabic word, which is a notation conven…

audit.recode_to: root/stem-initial, non-phonemic, quantity-insensitive (morphologically anchored initial stress) instead of 'weight-hedged'; the 'every long vowel (and diphthong)' clause demoted to Man/Ellis's and Portman's reading default for unmarked words; contra note: Blevins 2009 reads Man 1923's marks as 'not predictable' (final stress rare)
audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: the Temple 1903 p.115, Man/Ellis 1885 App. A and Portman 1898 p.29 passages are in the copies we hold at the stated places. But the classification rests on 19th/early-20th-century administrator grammars whose stress statements are transcription reading-defaults plus one generic 'Andamanese' sentence, while Glottolog's top item is a 2020 OUP reference grammar (Zamponi & Comrie, 440 pp) with a phonology chapter that, per its publisher abstract, explicitly treats Akabea stress and the reliability of the primary transcriptions. That chapter is paywalled and not yet obtained; the one open Comrie & Zamponi paper (Cadernos 2021) was downloaded to and is silent on stress. Since Z&C work from the same Man/Portman data, nothing seen suggests the weight-hedged coding is wrong, but it has not been checked against the only professional analysis

Our weight-hedged coding rests on 1885/1898/1903 transcription defaults plus one pan-Andamanese sentence; Z&C's reading of the same stress diacritics decides whether 'stress on every long vowel, else initial (root/stem)' stands, is reanalysed (e.g. root-based or lexical), or is declared unrecoverable.
